text: Greedy rules, the proofs that justify them, and the counterexamples that break them.

A **greedy** algorithm builds the answer one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never undoing it. It is short and fast, but only correct when you can prove a locally best choice never spoils the overall best answer.

items.p: Take any optimal answer that differs from greedy. Swap one piece to match greedy, and show it gets no worse.
After every step, greedy is at least as good as any other method so far.

text: With coins 4, 3, 1, greedy pays 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 needs only two. "Take the biggest coin" is correct for some coin systems (1, 2, 5, 10 …) and wrong for others.
Before trusting a greedy rule, compare it with a slow brute force on many small random inputs (a **stress test**). One mismatch kills the rule. No mismatches is evidence; then look for the proof.

title: Sort by a ratio: partial knapsack

text: Gold dust can be split, so **value per unit weight** is all that matters: take the richest pile first, then the next, and cut the last one to fit (P2240).
Compare ratios v₁/w₁ > v₂/w₂ as `v1 * w2 > v2 * w1`: exact in integers. When items cannot be split (0/1 knapsack) this greedy is wrong; that needs dynamic programming.

title: Two neighbours a and b in the queue

text: Only the pair's own waits change, so put the **shorter** one first.

Any order with a longer job before a shorter one can be improved by one swap, so sorted by time is optimal (P1223). `pair` sorts by the first field, then the second; `t[i].first` and `t[i].second` read the two fields.

Taking the contest that ends first leaves the most time for the rest; any optimal plan can swap its first contest for this one without losing anything (P1803). Sorting by start time or by length both fail on small examples.

title: More greedy rules from this list

text: Smallest number after deleting k digits: a digit larger than the one after it sits in a higher place, so deleting it helps most (P1106). Filling pits: a day of work covers one continuous stretch, so only each **rise** from the previous depth costs extra days (P5019).

Pairing: the most expensive souvenir must leave; let it take the cheapest one along if they fit. Two pointers after sorting (P1094). Adjacent sums: when a pair is too large, eating from the right box also lowers the next pair, so it is never worse (P3817).

Biggest number from concatenation: sort with `a + b > b + a` (P1012). The king's game sorts ministers by a × b and needs big numbers (P1080). Cheapest first (P1208, P1478) and alternating tallest and shortest jumps (P4995) are sort then scan greedies; prove each with an exchange of two neighbours.
Always merge the two smallest: priority queues and optimal codes.

**Huffman coding** gives frequent characters short codes and rare ones long codes. Build a tree: repeatedly take the **two smallest** weights, join them under a new node whose weight is their sum, and put it back. Each character's code length is its depth.
The total cost (sum of frequency × code length) equals the sum of all the joined weights. Why greedy works: the two rarest symbols can always sit deepest, as siblings, in some optimal tree.

`priority_queue` keeps the largest on top; with `greater<long long>` it keeps the smallest. push and pop cost O(log n), so n merges cost O(n log n). Merging fruit heaps (P1090) is exactly a Huffman tree.
Sorting once is not enough: each merged heap must go back among the others, possibly in the middle. That is why a priority queue is used.

Store the tree as a `parent` array: leaves are 0 … n − 1, and each merge creates the next node number. Following parents up from a leaf gives its depth, which is its code length. Check: 5·4 + 9·4 + 12·3 + 13·3 + 16·3 + 45·1 = 224.
